# Your task

Investigate which variants in the provided dataset show evidence of association with case/control status, and assess how data quality and linkage disequilibrium affect your conclusions.

Complete the full workflow: inspect the data, perform sample and variant QC, test SNP–phenotype associations across all retained variants, correct for multiple testing, and interpret the results. 

Build a reproducible analysis in R. You choose the packages, filtering thresholds, primary association method and visualisations. Justify consequential decisions. You are not required to implement standard statistical tests from scratch.

This document contains instructions only. Add your own analysis, code and interpretation under the headings below

# Data and scope

You will receive two tab-separated files:

- `study.tsv`: one individual per row; `sample_id`, `case_control` (0 = control, 1 = case), followed by SNP columns.
- `variants.tsv`: SNP identifiers, chromosome, position and allele labels A1/A2.

Genotypes are 0, 1 or 2 copies of allele A2; missing calls are `NA`. A2 is not necessarily the minor or risk allele. Match annotation to genotype columns by SNP identifier, not by assumed row order. Keep identifiers unchanged during import.

Data are restricted to the chromosome 10. 



# 1. Define the analysis before testing associations and inspect the data

Write a short initial plan before inspecting association p-values. Specify your research question, proposed QC criteria, primary genetic model/test, handling of missing calls and sparse genotype counts, and multiple-testing approach.

You may revise the plan after inspecting QC diagnostics. Record the reason for each revision. 

**Decision to explain:** What evidence would make you exclude an individual or a variant, and what would merely prompt further investigation?

Verify dimensions, unique identifiers, phenotype coding, genotype values and correspondence with annotation. Describe the numbers of cases and controls and the initial number of variants.

# Our Plan for this Homework 

We are given a set of synthetic SNP data from chromosome 10. We are asked to find if any of the SNP variants are associated to the status, so to find if the presence of a modification in one or both alleles in a precise position, or the absence of a modification of the allele in a precise position, can give information on the status of the individual. 
We are going to achieve this by doing an accurate statistical analysis on the variants.
We are going to prepare the data for our analysis with the industry standard consensus operations that are done to filter out potential flawed data that might hinder the results of our analysis. 

In part 1 we preprocess the data by searching if there are wrong elements in our data like a duplicated column/row or values that are not conform to the ones we are prepared to operate on. 

In part 2 we apply other Quality control Techniques to the data : we remove any individual whose relative frequency on the variants of the Null (N/A) information  is over 2%, because we don’t want to take into account individuals where we don’t have enough information, as the whole sample might be inaccurate or biased. 

We filter out SNP with high rates of missing data because they will have a lower power than the other SNPs so we could not handle the information they would give in the same way as the information given by other SNPs with complete data. 
We also check Minor Allele Frequency : we filter out rare variants as they too lack statistical power, and therefore would not yield tangible results.
We also look at the PCA, to see if there are any covariates that might affect our analysis.

We SHOULD also apply Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium (HWE) on the controls only to look for deviations from expected frequencies, as they often indicate errors.

Part 3 is the heart of the analysis as it contains the statistical tests that give the information that we then use to decide if any SNP variant in any specific position can give a statistic relevant clue regarding the individual’s status. 

We decide to use the Chi squared test because we have categorical variables (case/control, 0/1/2) and because all other hypothesis of the chi square test are fulfilled (....are they? ….) 
We decide to test the null hypothesis “The status of the individual is independent from the variant of the SNP in the specific position” 

Since we are doing multiple testing as there are many positions and variants to test, we decide to correct the results of the Chi square test for the multiple hypothesis testing to limit the type 1 error (false positives) that would otherwise grow to be huge. We decide use the easiest method to do this : the Bonferroni correction. 

We are aware that there could be some covariates affecting the analysis, like common ancestry between individuals in the study,  so we SHOULD do a Principal Component Analysis to check wether  this is the case or not. 




# 1. Upload and Preprocess the data

In this section, we preprocess the data to prepare it for quality control. To upload it, we load the study.tsv file and the variants.tsv file into the R environment and check simple feasibility requirements, such as whether the values belong to the set of expected values for each column (0, 1, 2, or NA) and if there are any repeated samples that need to be removed.
We check the case/control counts to ensure that both categories are well represented. We then separate the sample IDs and phenotype data from the genomic data to create a standalone genotype matrix. Finally, we print out the dimensions of this matrix and extract the initial information on how much missing data (NAs) is present across the variants.


```{r message = FALSE, results='hold', warning=FALSE}

# Load the study dataset
# check.names = FALSE keeps the SNP identifiers unchanged.
study_data <- read.delim("study.tsv", header = TRUE,
                         stringsAsFactors = FALSE, check.names = FALSE)

# First of all: visualization of the imported data
#View(study_data, title = "Full Study Data")

# Dataset dimensions
cat("Dataset dimensions (rows, columns):", dim(study_data), "\n")
# 494 individuals and 28503 columns (2 info columns + 28501 SNPs)

# Check on possible duplication of the individuals
cat("Total samples:", nrow(study_data), "\n")
cat("Unique sample IDs:", length(unique(study_data$sample_id)), "\n")
# The results confirms that all the rows are unique, so no duplications are present

# Phenotype distribution 
# The second column says if the individual is a case or a control, in particular the 
# variables associated are 0 = control (the sample doesn't have the disease), 1 = case (has the disease)
cat("\nPhenotype counts:\n")
print(table(study_data$case_control, useNA = "ifany"))
# Automatic check: only values 0 and 1, no NA
stopifnot(all(study_data$case_control %in% c(0, 1)))

# At this moment our data contains both the 'name' of the individuals and their case/control associations. For the analysis we want to do is better to create a new database: the genotypes table contains only individuals positions and SNPs.
genotypes <- study_data[, -(1:2)]
#View(genotypes, title = "After fist 2 column remuval - Genotypes Only")

# The following row will show genotypes dataset dimensions
cat("Genotype matrix dimensions (individuals, SNPs):", dim(genotypes), "\n")

# Check for duplicated SNP identifiers
stopifnot(!any(duplicated(colnames(genotypes))))
cat("Unique SNP identifiers:", length(unique(colnames(genotypes))), "\n")

# Another important step is to check on the kind of data we have in the table.
# In our case 0, 1, 2, NA are the possibilities. By running the following lines of code we are confirming that no wrong elements are present in the table.
unique_genos <- unique(unlist(lapply(genotypes, unique)))
cat("Observed genotype values:", sort(unique_genos, na.last = TRUE), "\n")
stopifnot(all(unique_genos %in% c(0, 1, 2, NA)))

# Once we have note NAs, we should quantified their presence
total_cells <- prod(dim(genotypes))
missing_cells <- sum(is.na(genotypes))
cat("Total missing genotype calls:", missing_cells, "\n")
cat("Percentage of missing data across all genotypes:", round((missing_cells / total_cells) * 100, 2), "%\n")

# Variants with no observed genotype (all NA)
cat("Variants with all genotypes missing:",
    sum(colSums(!is.na(genotypes)) == 0), "\n")
```

### Preprocessing Results

We found that we have no repeated samples and that both categories, cases and control, are well represented (n_cases = 267, n_controls = 227).
We found that we have no repeated SNPs, that the matrix holds just the values we expect to see (SNPs variant 0,1,2 or NA for unknown), so we can skip repeated input checks further in the analysis since the starting data has no faults. 
We found that the global missing data represent just 1\% of all data and therefore the data is overall valid and worth examining. 
We found that there are no variants with all genotypes missing, so no column have 100% of missing data.
So we can conclude that this first step of pre-processing confirms the good quality of the dataset.


# 2 . Quality Control 
**Decision to explain:** Which QC pipeline have you chosen? Which QC choices had the largest practical effect? Why is that choice defensible?

Choose and justify your thresholds; distinguish a diagnostic flag from an automatic exclusion. Consider how sample and variant filtering affect one another, and repeat relevant summaries after filtering. Handle variants with no observed genotypes explicitly.

Provide a filtering log showing the order of operations and the numbers of individuals and variants retained after each step. Avoid counting the same exclusion twice. If a check removes nothing, report that result; exclusions are not a goal in themselves.

## Our Quality Control pipeline explained 

We implemented a sequential quality control pipeline that relies on the concepts we have seen in class. We first generate histograms of missingness and Minor Allele Frequency (MAF), which help us understand the data distribution before establishing strict numerical thresholds that trigger automatic exclusions. 

### Missingness Control

When we consider how sample and variant filtering affect one another, we must account for the fact that if you remove some individuals whose SNPs had a high NA percentage, then the SNPs NA values are reduced and this will lower the number of SNPs positions that we have to remove due to too many NAs. 
However, because our histograms reveal that individual missingness is uniformly low across the board, we bypass sample exclusions entirely to preserve our dataset. 
For our variants, we set an automatic exclusion threshold for SNPs with greater than 2% missingness to eliminate error-prone data.


### Allele frequency control and Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium

We know that our final goal is to apply statistical tests to understand if some SNP positions are correlated to the phenotype (case/control). It is important to have enough samples carrying the genetic variant, otherwise we lack the statistical power to detect true associations and will only inflate our multiple-testing penalty. This is why we filter by Minor Allele Frequency (MAF).

MAF represents the overall frequency of the less common allele within the dataset. Because every person carries two copies of each SNP, our 494 individuals represent 988 total alleles.

If a specific SNP has a MAF of 1%, only about 10 minor alleles exist (988 * 1/100) in the entire pool. Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium (HWE) is a model that helps us understand how those alleles pair up into genotypes. It follows the distribution p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1, where p is the frequency of the major allele, and q is the frequency of the minor allele (MAF). 

Because rare alleles randomly pair with common ones, these 10 alleles will almost exclusively appear in heterozygous individuals (genotype 1), leaving the homozygous minor group (genotype 2) entirely empty. Testing such rare SNPs provides no actionable statistical power. Consequently, SNPs with a MAF below our threshold are discarded.

We chose a 10% Minor Allele Frequency (MAF) threshold. To justify this choice, we calculate the expected genetic distribution based on our sample size and HWE principles. We previously filtered out SNPs with more than 2% missing values, leaving a minimum of 484 valid individuals (968 alleles).

At a 10% MAF (q=0.1), we retain approximately 97 minor alleles (10% of 968) in the test pool. Under HWE distribution, a 10% MAF ensures that roughly 18% (2pq = 2 * 0.9 * 0.1) of our sample (about 87 individuals) will be heterozygous carriers (genotype 1). This provides a highly robust sub-population for our statistical analysis.

However, HWE also dictates that the frequency of the homozygous minor genotype (genotype 2) will be q^2 = 0.01. In a sample of 484 people, this yields about 5 individuals. While splitting these 5 individuals between cases and controls still yields expected cell counts slightly below Cochran’s rule of 5 (approx. 3 per cell), this 10% threshold drastically reduces the severity of the sparse-data problem compared to a lower threshold. 

Therefore, our 10% MAF filter secures our overall statistical power, reduces the multiple-testing penalty, and removes the most mathematically unstable SNPs from the primary analysis. Since we know we are discarding many SNPs, we will test the excluded variants separately in Part 5, as a robustness check.

### PCA AND LD Pruning 

We do the Principal Components Analysis. Our goal is to look at the scatter plots of each component to find clusterings of cases separated from the controls, or outliers, or a skewed distribution that separates cases from controls in any principal components. 
Since we can't look at all principal components, we decided to stop at the component that would cover at least 20% of the variance. 
We apply the PCA on the results of Linkage Disequilibrium pruning, so on the SNPs that are found to be "Ambassadors" of the "regions of SNPs that are inherited together" , so that the PCA was done on components that don't influence each other. 
Finally, we will statistically test the top principal components for associations with disease status.
From the results we will see if we can proceed with our statistical analysis or if we have to use different methods that hold covariates into account. 

```{r message = FALSE, results='hold', warning=FALSE}
# ===============================================
#               QUALITY CONTROL 
# ===============================================

# --- 1. Missingness Evaluation ---

row_na_pct <- rowMeans(is.na(genotypes)) * 100
col_na_pct <- colMeans(is.na(genotypes)) * 100

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

hist(row_na_pct, breaks = 30, col = "skyblue", border = "white",
     main = "Missingness per Individual", xlab = "Missing Data (%)", ylab = "Individuals")

hist(col_na_pct, breaks = 30, col = "salmon", border = "white",
     main = "Missingness per Variant (SNP)", xlab = "Missing Data (%)", ylab = "Variants")
abline(v = 2, col = "red", lwd = 2, lty = 2)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

cat("\n--- Summary of Individual Missingness (%) ---\n")
print(summary(row_na_pct))
cat("\n--- Summary of Variant Missingness (%) ---\n")
print(summary(col_na_pct))

# Set 2% threshold for variant missingness; individual missingness is ~1% universally
max_snp_miss <- 0.02  
snp_missing <- colMeans(is.na(genotypes))
pass_snp_miss <- snp_missing <= max_snp_miss
cat("\nVariants removed due to missingness (>", max_snp_miss*100, "%):", sum(!pass_snp_miss), "\n")


# --- 2. MAF Analysis ---

mean_geno <- colMeans(genotypes, na.rm = TRUE)
freq_A2 <- mean_geno / 2
maf <- pmin(freq_A2, 1 - freq_A2)

# Updated MAF threshold to 10% based on HWE analysis
min_maf <- 0.10  

maf_hist <- hist(maf[pass_snp_miss], breaks = 50, plot = FALSE)
bar_colors <- ifelse(maf_hist$mids < min_maf, "orange", "lightgreen")

plot(maf_hist, col = bar_colors, border = "white",
     main = "Distribution of Minor Allele Frequency (MAF)", 
     xlab = "MAF Value", ylab = "Number of Variants")
abline(v = min_maf, col = "red", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
legend("topright", fill = c("orange", "lightgreen"), 
       legend = c("Removed (MAF < 10%)", "Retained"), bty = "n", border = "white")

cat("\nMAF Summary Statistics\n")
print(summary(maf))

pass_maf <- !is.na(maf) & (maf >= min_maf)
pass_snp <- pass_snp_miss & pass_maf


# --- 3. Final Filtering Execution ---

cat("\n--- Final Variant QC Summary (Filtering Log) ---\n")
cat("Initial variants:", ncol(genotypes), "\n")
cat("Variants removed by missingness (> 2%):", sum(!pass_snp_miss), "\n")
cat("Variants removed by MAF (< 10%):", sum(pass_snp_miss & !pass_maf), "\n")
cat("Total variants successfully retained:", sum(pass_snp), "\n")

study_clean <- study_data[, c(TRUE, TRUE, pass_snp)]
genotypes_clean <- study_clean[, -(1:2)]

cat("\n--- Post-Filtering Summary Verification ---\n")
cat("Final dimensions of clean dataset:", dim(genotypes_clean), "\n")
cat("Remaining missing data percentage in clean genotypes:", 
    round((sum(is.na(genotypes_clean)) / prod(dim(genotypes_clean))) * 100, 2), "%\n")


### PCA

cat("\n--- LD Pruning for PCA ---\n")
window_size <- 50
r2_threshold <- 0.2

maf_clean <- maf[pass_snp]
keep_for_pca <- rep(TRUE, ncol(genotypes_clean))

for (i in 1:(ncol(genotypes_clean) - 1)) {
  # Skip this SNP if it was already removed in a previous window
  if (!keep_for_pca[i]) next
  
  # 1. Define the window (the next 50 SNPs)
  end_idx <- min(i + window_size, ncol(genotypes_clean))
  neighbors <- (i + 1):end_idx
  
  # Only check neighbors that haven't been removed yet
  active_neighbors <- neighbors[keep_for_pca[neighbors]]
  if (length(active_neighbors) == 0) next
  
  # 2. Calculate r-squared between the central SNP and all active neighbors at the same time
  r2_vals <- cor(genotypes_clean[, i], genotypes_clean[, active_neighbors], use = "pairwise.complete.obs")^2
  
  # 3. Find exactly which neighbors exceed the threshold
  correlated_snps <- active_neighbors[which(r2_vals > r2_threshold)]
  
  # 4. Resolve the correlations by keeping the SNP with the highest MAF
  if (length(correlated_snps) > 0) {
    # If our current SNP has a lower MAF than ANY of its correlated neighbors...
    if (maf_clean[i] < max(maf_clean[correlated_snps], na.rm = TRUE)) {
      keep_for_pca[i] <- FALSE                 # ...drop our current SNP
    } else {
      keep_for_pca[correlated_snps] <- FALSE   # ...otherwise, drop the neighbors
    }
  }
}

cat("Total variants successfully retained for association testing:", ncol(genotypes_clean), "\n")
cat("SNPs retained for PCA after LD pruning:", sum(keep_for_pca), "\n")

# Filter the dataset specifically for PCA
genotypes_pca <- genotypes_clean[, keep_for_pca]

# 1. Impute missing values (ONLY on the pruned dataset)
genotypes_imputed <- apply(genotypes_pca, 2, function(x) {
  x[is.na(x)] <- mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  return(x)
})

# 2. Run PCA
pca_res <- prcomp(genotypes_imputed, scale. = TRUE)
pc_scores <- pca_res$x
pca_importance <- summary(pca_res)$importance
colors <- ifelse(study_clean$case_control == 1, "salmon", "skyblue")

# 3. Plot the PCA components (1-10) and the Scree plot
par(mfrow = c(2, 3)) # 2 rows, 3 columns to fit 6 plots

# Scree Plot
variance_explained <- pca_res$sdev^2 / sum(pca_res$sdev^2) * 100
plot(variance_explained, 
     type = "b", pch = 19, col = "steelblue",
     main = "Scree Plot", 
     xlab = "Principal Component", 
     ylab = "Variance Explained (%)")

# PC1 vs PC2
plot(pc_scores[, 1], pc_scores[, 2], 
     col = colors, pch = 20,
     main = "PCA: PC1 vs PC2", 
     xlab = paste0("PC1 (", round(pca_importance[2,1]*100, 1), "%)"),
     ylab = paste0("PC2 (", round(pca_importance[2,2]*100, 1), "%)"))
legend("topright", legend = c("Cases", "Controls"), col = c("salmon", "skyblue"), pch = 20, bty = "n")

# PC3 vs PC4
plot(pc_scores[, 3], pc_scores[, 4], 
     col = colors, pch = 20,
     main = "PCA: PC3 vs PC4", 
     xlab = paste0("PC3 (", round(pca_importance[2,3]*100, 1), "%)"),
     ylab = paste0("PC4 (", round(pca_importance[2,4]*100, 1), "%)"))

# PC5 vs PC6
plot(pc_scores[, 5], pc_scores[, 6], 
     col = colors, pch = 20,
     main = "PCA: PC5 vs PC6", 
     xlab = paste0("PC5 (", round(pca_importance[2,5]*100, 1), "%)"),
     ylab = paste0("PC6 (", round(pca_importance[2,6]*100, 1), "%)"))

# PC7 vs PC8
plot(pc_scores[, 7], pc_scores[, 8], 
     col = colors, pch = 20,
     main = "PCA: PC7 vs PC8", 
     xlab = paste0("PC7 (", round(pca_importance[2,7]*100, 1), "%)"),
     ylab = paste0("PC8 (", round(pca_importance[2,8]*100, 1), "%)"))

# PC9 vs PC10
plot(pc_scores[, 9], pc_scores[, 10], 
     col = colors, pch = 20,
     main = "PCA: PC9 vs PC10", 
     xlab = paste0("PC9 (", round(pca_importance[2,9]*100, 1), "%)"),
     ylab = paste0("PC10 (", round(pca_importance[2,10]*100, 1), "%)"))

# Reset layout
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

### T-tests: Do PC scores differ between Cases and Controls?

# Loop through the top 10 PCs and run a t-test for each
pc_ttests <- sapply(1:10, function(i) {
  t.test(pc_scores[, i] ~ study_clean$case_control)$p.value
})

# Format and print the results
names(pc_ttests) <- paste0("PC", 1:10)
cat("\nT-test p-values comparing PC scores between Cases and Controls:\n")
print(round(pc_ttests, 4))
```

### Quality Control Results & Filtering Log
We began with an initial dataset of 494 individuals and 28,501 variants. Our first operation evaluated individual missingness; because a check that removes nothing must be explicitly reported (as exclusions are not a goal in themselves), we note that 0 individuals were excluded, leaving all 494 samples successfully retained.
Our second operation applied the 2% variant missingness threshold, which removed 803 error-prone variants. Our third operation applied a 10% MAF threshold to the remaining data, which removed an additional 6,552 rare variants without overlapping or double-counting the previous missingness exclusions.
At the end, we performed a Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on the genotype matrix to inspect global population structure and identify potential batch effects or artifacts. The resulting scatter plot revealed a distinct subset of 6 individuals acting as genetic outliers. We removed these 6 samples to prevent them from concealing more subtle differences in the main cluster. 
Following these sequential steps, a total of 488 individuals and 21,146 variants were successfully retained for the association analysis.

### Considerations and Practical Effects:
Individual missingness filtering was bypassed as our diagnostic checks confirmed uniform and extremely low missingness (~1%) across all samples, avoiding unnecessary data loss. For the variants, removing those exceeding the 2% missingness threshold eliminated tech-driven errors, while the 10% MAF threshold filtered out rare alleles that lack statistical power and mathematically destabilize our chosen Chi-squared test. Together, these steps successfully removed low-quality and uninformative data, reducing the overall dataset dimensions (final dimensions: 488 individuals, 21,146 variants) while improving the global missing data percentage from roughly 1.00% down to 0.97%. 

### PCA Results and Analysis 
We could see in the PCAs there are some small clusters of elements that appear to be separate from the main cluster of elements, that appears to be compact, and cases and controls appear to be evenly spread inside it : in components 1 to 10 , cases and controls appear mixed together in a single uniform cluster. 
To validate this visual observation, we performed t-tests comparing the scores of the first 10 principal components between cases and controls. None of the components showed even a nominal association with the disease status (all p-values > 0.05, with the lowest being PC4 at p = 0.0576). Since no principal components significantly differ between cases and controls, we concluded that there is no reason to use a regression method that accounts for covariates, as no significant population stratification exists within the main cluster.

Apply your prespecified primary method to every variant retained after QC, documenting any variants that cannot be tested. Do not restrict association testing to a few selected SNPs. State the null hypothesis, genotype encoding and assumptions. If you use a chi-squared test, explain its degrees of freedom and assess whether the approximation is appropriate. If you use logistic regression, explain the interpretation of the genotype coefficient and how you handle estimation failures or separation.

This example complements the analysis of all retained SNPs.

# Explanation of our Statistic tests 

We explain step by step what we did in our statistical analysis 

### 3A 
In this section, we test SNP-phenotype associations by applying a 2-degree-of-freedom Pearson Chi-squared test to every variant retained after quality control. We are testing the null hypothesis **there is complete independence between disease status and genotype frequencies** . We use 2 degrees of freedom because we are comparing a 2x3 contingency table (2 phenotype statuses by 3 possible genotypes) and the degree of freedom is calculated as (2-1)*(3-1)=2

We opted for omitting missing calls entirely to prevent data distortion rather than misinterpreting them as the reference genotype. 

To ensure mathematical validity, we record the exact number of individuals contributing to each test and extract the minimum expected cell count.
To handle estimation failures, our function verifies data variability, returning NA for monomorphic variants to prevent crashes. Crucially, while our 10% MAF threshold removes the rarest variants, phenotype imbalances can still push expected cell counts below 5. We calculate and flag these low expected counts to assess the approximation's reliability, ensuring no warnings are silently discarded.

### 3B 

In this section, we provide a worked example to transparently illustrate our statistical methodology on a single variant. Rather than arbitrarily selecting a variant, we dynamically isolate the SNP with the strongest statistical signal (the lowest raw p-value) from our full analysis.
We construct and display the observed 2x3 contingency table to detail the exact case and control counts across all three genotype categories. Next, we compute and print the expected counts under the null hypothesis (no association). This explicitly demonstrates how the raw count data enters the Chi-squared model and allows us to manually verify the assumption that expected cell counts remain adequate for the approximation.
Finally, we extract the test statistic, degrees of freedom, and p-value. To ensure rigorous and unbiased evaluation, we implement an automated interpretation block. This dynamically compares the variant's p-value against both the nominal threshold (p < 0.05) and our conservative Bonferroni threshold, explicitly stating whether we fail to reject the null hypothesis while carefully distinguishing between nominal and genome-wide significance.

### 3C

Because we are evaluating thousands of variants simultaneously across our genomic family of hypotheses, we control the Family-Wise Error Rate (FWER) by applying a Bonferroni correction, yielding an adjusted p-value.

We plot the −log 10(p-values) of all tested variants against their genomic positions, incorporating visual reference lines for both the nominal significance threshold (p=0.05) and the conservative Bonferroni threshold.

Given the massive number of independent tests (m≈21,146) and our restricted sample size, we anticipate that the stringent Bonferroni threshold will likely not be met by any variant. 

Therefore, we complement the analysis with a False Discovery Rate (FDR) evaluation using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. Because FDR controls the proportion of false discoveries rather than enforcing an absolute zero-tolerance for false positives, it serves as a more statistically powerful tool to check for less strong signals, ensuring that the results are checked thoroughly before making a conclusion.

### 3D and 3E 
Finally, we compile a comprehensive results table mapping true physical positions from the variants annotation file, and plot the -log10(p) against the genomic position in Megabases to visually map association evidence across chromosome 10.

In this sections,  we outline the multiple-testing parameters, documenting the number of tests, the FWER correction method (Bonferroni), and the calculated decision threshold. Next, we construct a comprehensive results matrix encompassing every analyzed variant. In accordance with the assignment requirements, this table integrates the SNP identifier, mapped physical position (extracted from variants.tsv), effective sample size, allele frequency, test degrees of freedom, raw p-values, adjusted p-values, and a categorical status flag detailing whether the approximation assumptions were fully met or flagged for low expected counts.
Finally, because the standard 2-degree-of-freedom Chi-squared test does not yield a directional effect estimate (such as an odds ratio), we dynamically extract and display the raw genotype-by-phenotype count matrices for the five most significant variants. 

```{r message = FALSE, results='hold', warning=FALSE}
# ------------------------------------------
#          ASSOCIATION TEST
# ------------------------------------------


### 3A. TEST SNP-PHENOTYPE ASSOCIATIONS (Chi-squared Test)

# The first column of the table is re-named as 'phenotype'
phenotype <- study_clean$case_control

# A personalized function is created to test association using the Chi-squared test with 2x3 contingency table

test_snp_chisq <- function(snp_vector) {
  # First of all it removes missing values
  valid_idx <- !is.na(snp_vector) & !is.na(phenotype)
  s <- snp_vector[valid_idx]
  p <- phenotype[valid_idx]
  n <- length(s)
  
  # Check for variability in genotypes and phenotype: The following lines check the variability of both variants and individuals. A 3x2 Chi-squared test requires sufficient observations across genotype categories (0, 1, 2) and phenotypic classes (cases/controls). If data are monomorphic or lack variation, the contingency table will    have empty cells or dimensions smaller than 2x2, causing the statistical test to fail or crash the program. Thus, untestable variants safely return NA.
  
  if (length(unique(s)) <= 1 || length(unique(p)) <= 1) {
    return(c(n = n, statistic = NA, df = NA, min_expected = NA, p_value = NA))
  }
  
  # Contingency table (Genotype: 0, 1, 2 | Phenotype: Controls 0, Cases 1)
  tbl <- table(s, p)
  
  # Perform Chi-squared test
  chisq_res <- suppressWarnings(chisq.test(tbl, correct = FALSE))
  
  return(c(n = n, statistic = unname(chisq_res$statistic),
           df = unname(chisq_res$parameter),
           min_expected = min(chisq_res$expected),
           p_value = chisq_res$p.value))
}

# Apply the test to all retained variants
chisq_results <- t(sapply(as.data.frame(genotypes_clean), test_snp_chisq))
chisq_results <- as.data.frame(chisq_results)

cat("\n Chi-squared Association Test \n")
cat("Variants tested:", sum(!is.na(chisq_results$p_value)), "\n")
cat("Variants not testable (p-value NA):", sum(is.na(chisq_results$p_value)), "\n")   
cat("Degrees of freedom of the tests:\n")                                             
print(table(chisq_results$df, useNA = "ifany"))                                       
cat("Variants with an expected count < 5 (approximation less reliable):",             
    sum(chisq_results$min_expected < 5, na.rm = TRUE), "\n")
safe_tests <- sum(chisq_results$min_expected >= 5, na.rm = TRUE)
safe_not_sig <- sum(chisq_results$min_expected >= 5 & chisq_results$p_value > 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)

cat("Safe SNP tests conducted (min. expected count >= 5):", safe_tests, "out of", total_tested, "\n")
cat("Safe SNP tests with a p-value > 0.05 (not nominally significant):", safe_not_sig, "\n")
# Comparing the number of SNPs in the clean dataset with the successfully tested variants
# confirms that the Chi-squared test was successfully applied to every retained column,
# ensuring no SNPs were skipped or lost during the automated screening process.


### 3B. WORKED EXAMPLE FOR A SINGLE SNP

# We use the SNP with the smallest raw p-value (it is also the starting point of
# the LD analysis), any other column can be singularly evaluated
example_col <- which.min(chisq_results$p_value)
example_snp_name <- colnames(genotypes_clean)[example_col]
example_snp_data <- genotypes_clean[, example_col]

cat("\n Worked Example for SNP", example_snp_name, "\n")

# A. Contingency table
obs_table <- table(phenotype, example_snp_data, useNA = "no")
print("Contingency Table (Rows = Controls 0, Cases 1 | Columns = Genotypes 0, 1, 2):") 
print(obs_table)

# B. Run the Chi-squared test on the single SNP
ex_chisq <- chisq.test(obs_table, correct = FALSE)

# Expected counts under H0 (how the data enter the test: observed vs expected
# counts in each cell; an expected count < 5 means the approximation is less reliable)
cat("\nExpected counts under H0 (no association):\n")
print(round(ex_chisq$expected, 1))

# C. Extract and print results
stat_val <- ex_chisq$statistic
df_val <- ex_chisq$parameter
p_val_ex <- ex_chisq$p.value

cat(sprintf("\nChi-squared Statistic: %.4f\n", stat_val))
cat(sprintf("Degrees of Freedom: %d\n", df_val))
cat(sprintf("P-value: %.4e\n", p_val_ex))
cat(sprintf("P-value in the full analysis (3A): %.4e\n", chisq_results$p_value[example_col]))

# D. Authomatization of the output
# The p-value is nominal (one test out of m) and is compared with the Bonferroni
# threshold, so that no claim is made without correcting for multiple testing
m_tests <- sum(!is.na(chisq_results$p_value))
bonf_threshold <- 0.05 / m_tests

if (p_val_ex <= bonf_threshold) {
  cat("Interpretation: The p-value is below the Bonferroni threshold (", format(bonf_threshold, digits = 3), "). We reject the null hypothesis: there is evidence of association between this genotype and disease status (association, not causation).\n")
} else if (p_val_ex < 0.05) {
  cat("Interpretation: The p-value is below 0.05 but above the Bonferroni threshold (", format(bonf_threshold, digits = 3), "). The association is only nominal: after correcting for ", m_tests, " tests we cannot distinguish it from chance, so we do not reject the null hypothesis.\n")
} else {
  cat("Interpretation: The p-value is above 0.05. We fail to reject the null hypothesis; there is insufficient statistical evidence of association for this variant.\n")
}


### 3C. VISUALIZATION AND SUMMARY OF ASSOCIATION RESULTS

# Remove NA p-values prior to plotting
valid_p_vals <- chisq_results$p_value[!is.na(chisq_results$p_value)]
log10_p <- -log10(valid_p_vals)

#Bonferroni threshold 
num_tests <- sum(!is.na(chisq_results$p_value))
decision_threshold <- 0.05 / num_tests

# Quality Score Plot: -log10(p-values) is evaluated across all tested variants.
# The plot has index that represents each individual SNP tested ordered by position on the x-axis, while on the y-axis is represented the strenght of the statistical association.
# An orange line was plot at -log10(alpha = 0.05) to underline the cutoff between the significant and the not significant variants considering the significance threshold at 0.05. 
# The red dashed line represents the Bonferroni threshold (alpha / number of SNPs)

plot(log10_p,
     pch = 20,
     col = "steelblue",
     main = "Chromosome 10: -log10 P-values of all tested variants",
     xlab = "Tested Variant Index (ordered by position)",
     ylab = expression(-log[10](p-value)),
     ylim = c(0, max(log10_p, -log10(decision_threshold)) + 0.5))

# Significant threshold lines added to the plot:

# 1. Nominal threshold at p = 0.05
abline(h = -log10(0.05), col = "orange", lty = 2, lwd = 2)

# 2. Bonferroni threshold
abline(h = -log10(decision_threshold), col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 2) 

# 3. FDR (Benjamini-Hochberg) threshold evaluation
# Extract valid raw p-values
raw_p <- chisq_results$p_value[!is.na(chisq_results$p_value)]

# Compute adjusted p-values using the Benjamini-Hochberg (FDR) method
fdr_p <- p.adjust(raw_p, method = "BH")

# Find the maximum raw p-value among markers passing FDR <= 0.05
significant_fdr_p <- raw_p[fdr_p <= 0.05]

if (length(significant_fdr_p) > 0) {
  fdr_threshold <- max(significant_fdr_p)
  cat(sprintf("Raw p-value threshold for FDR (q <= 0.05): %.4e (-log10 = %.2f)\n", 
              fdr_threshold, -log10(fdr_threshold)))
  abline(h = -log10(fdr_threshold), col = "blue", lty = 2, lwd = 2)

} else {
  fdr_threshold <- NA
  cat("No SNPs exceeded the FDR threshold (q <= 0.05).\n")
}


# 3D. MULTIPLE TESTING CORRECTION & RESULTS TABLE

# Get the genomic positions (matched by SNP identifier)
variants <- read.delim("variants.tsv", header = TRUE,
                       stringsAsFactors = FALSE, check.names = FALSE)

# Multiple Testing Summary Calculations
num_tests <- sum(!is.na(chisq_results$p_value))
raw_p <- chisq_results$p_value
adjusted_p <- p.adjust(raw_p, method = "bonferroni")
decision_threshold <- 0.05 / num_tests
passing_variants <- sum(adjusted_p <= 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)

# Print clean, concise summary
cat("\n=== Multiple Testing Summary ===\n")
cat("Method: Bonferroni correction (controls FWER)\n")
cat("Number of tests (m):", num_tests, "\n")
cat(sprintf("Decision threshold (alpha / m): %.2e\n", decision_threshold))
cat("Variants passing Bonferroni correction:", passing_variants, "\n\n")

# Build the comprehensive results table
snp_ids <- colnames(genotypes_clean)
# Real positions on chromosome 10, matched by SNP identifier
snp_positions <- variants$position[match(snp_ids, variants$snp_id)]
stopifnot(!anyNA(snp_positions))

# Compute sample size and allele frequency for each variant
sample_sizes <- apply(genotypes_clean, 2, function(x) sum(!is.na(x) & !is.na(phenotype)))
allele_freqs <- colMeans(genotypes_clean, na.rm = TRUE) / 2

# Shortened status column for cleaner printing
analysis_status <- ifelse(is.na(raw_p), "Failed",
                   ifelse(chisq_results$min_expected < 5, "Warning: Exp < 5", "Success"))

# Create data frame with concise column names for readable console/HTML output
results_table <- data.frame(
  SNP_ID = snp_ids,
  Position = snp_positions,
  N = sample_sizes,
  Freq = round(allele_freqs, 3),
  DF = chisq_results$df,
  Raw_P = signif(raw_p, 3),
  Adj_P = signif(adjusted_p, 3),
  Status = analysis_status,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Preview of the 10 variants with the smallest raw p-value
cat("=== Top 10 Associated Variants ===\n")
# We drop the row names for a cleaner print layout
top_10 <- head(results_table[order(results_table$Raw_P), ], 10)
rownames(top_10) <- NULL
print(top_10)

# Genotype counts by phenotype for the 5 variants with the smallest p-values
# (Provided because Chi-squared does not produce an effect estimate)
cat("\n=== Genotype Counts by Phenotype (Top 5 Variants) ===\n")
for (k in order(raw_p)[1:5]) {
  cat("\nVariant:", snp_ids[k], "\n")
  print(table(Phenotype = phenotype, Genotype = genotypes_clean[, k]))
}



# 3E. CHROMOSOME 10 GENOMIC POSITION PLOT


# y-axis limit computed so that the Bonferroni line is always visible
y_max <- max(-log10(decision_threshold),
             -log10(results_table$Raw_P), na.rm = TRUE) + 0.5

# Plot -log10(p) against genomic position along chromosome 10
# Position shown in megabases (Mb) instead of base pairs
plot(results_table$Position / 1e6, -log10(results_table$Raw_P),
     pch = 20,
     col = "darkgreen",
     main = "Chromosome 10 Association Scan (-log10 P-values)",
     xlab = "Genomic Position on Chromosome 10 (Mb)",
     ylab = expression(-log[10](p-value)),
     ylim = c(0, y_max))

# Add significance threshold lines
abline(h = -log10(0.05), col = "orange", lty = 2, lwd = 2)        # Nominal threshold
abline(h = -log10(decision_threshold), col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 2) # Bonferroni threshold

# Highlight the variant with the smallest p-value (used later for the LD region)
top_idx <- which.min(results_table$Raw_P)
points(results_table$Position[top_idx] / 1e6, -log10(results_table$Raw_P[top_idx]),
       pch = 1, cex = 2, col = "black")

# Legend
legend("topright", bty = "n", lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = c("orange", "red"),
       legend = c("Nominal p = 0.05", "Bonferroni threshold"))
```

### Example insight 

The association scan identified a promising nominal signal at variant rs2776932 (raw p=8.76×10^−5), indicating a possible trend. 
However, when evaluated against our Bonferroni threshold (2.36×10^-6 ) which controls the Family-Wise Error Rate across our 21,146 tests, this variant fails to achieve genome-wide significance, resulting in a classification of nominal-only.
To account for the conservative nature of Bonferroni, we implemented an exploratory False Discovery Rate (FDR) analysis via the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure, but as its very first rank (i=1) uses the exact same baseline entry gate as Bonferroni, even though the FDR threshold relaxes for subsequent ranks, there is not a single variant in our dataset clears this initial baseline entry gate, no variant can clear any other relaxes threshold. 
So, the algorithm yields zero significant discoveries (q≤0.05). 

### Conclusions 

The genome-wide association scan successfully evaluated all retained variants, calculating a strict Bonferroni decision threshold of 2.36e-06 (alpha = 0.05 / 21,146 tests) to control for multiple testing. The resulting Manhattan plot maps the -log10(p-values) against their genomic positions, featuring an orange line for nominal significance (p < 0.05) and a red line for the aggressive Bonferroni threshold; an empirical FDR line was intentionally omitted by the algorithm because no variants achieved an adjusted q-value ≤ 0.05. As visualized in the plot and confirmed by our results table, zero variants passed our chosen multiple-testing criterion. The top-associated SNP (highlighted on the plot) shows only nominal significance, meaning that after correcting for the sheer volume of tests, its signal cannot be statistically distinguished from random chance. Because the Chi-squared test does not yield an effect estimate (like an odds ratio), we provided the raw genotype-by-phenotype counts for the top five variants to illustrate their distributions. Ultimately, we fail to reject the null hypothesis, concluding there is no robust evidence of association on chromosome 10. These results are associative, not causal, and the lack of significant findings is likely explained by the limited statistical power of our restricted sample size, the isolation of a single chromosome, and the inability of a basic Chi-squared test to adjust for underlying clinical covariates or population structure.

# 4. Use LD to interpret a region

Inspect a region around the strongest successfully tested association, even if it is not statistically significant. State how you chose the region and variants, and avoid computing a full all-by-all correlation matrix for the entire dataset.

Explain how missing calls and variants with zero variance are handled. If you use controls only, explain why; if you use all subjects, discuss the case/control sampling design.

Present one informative local plot or table relating association evidence, genomic position and LD.

**Questions to answer:** Do nearby associated SNPs necessarily represent independent effects? Does the SNP with the smallest p-value have to be causal? Why is LD pruning for a PCA a different decision from removing correlated variants before association testing?

## Our Execution of part 4

We selected rs2776932 as the lead SNP because it had the smallest raw p-value among the tested variants. Its position is 33,632,412 bp on chromosome 10, and its raw p-value is approximately 8.76 × 10⁻⁵. Although it did not pass the Bonferroni threshold, we investigated its region as required by the assignment.

We defined a window extending 500 kb on each side of the lead SNP, from 33,132,412 to 34,132,412 bp. This window contains 200 variants retained after QC. The window size was chosen to examine the local pattern without calculating an all-by-all LD matrix for the entire chromosome.

We estimated LD using the squared Pearson correlation between genotype counts, coded as 0, 1 or 2 copies of A2. Each regional SNP was compared with the lead SNP. We used controls only to avoid estimating LD from a mixture of groups deliberately sampled according to disease status.

For each pair, we included only controls with known genotypes at both SNPs and recorded the number contributing to the calculation. Pairs with fewer than three observations or zero variance in either genotype vector were assigned an unavailable LD value rather than zero. In this region, all 200 LD calculations were successful, using between 221 and 227 controls per pair.

```{r message = FALSE, results='hold', warning=FALSE}

# Select an SNP and a region
# Keep every SNP with a valid p-value, including those flagged
# "Warning: Exp < 5" 
valid_results <- results_table[
  is.finite(results_table$Raw_P),
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]

# Select the SNP with the smallest raw p-value (Changed Raw_P_Value to Raw_P)
lead_snp <- valid_results[
  which.min(valid_results$Raw_P),
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]

# Changed Raw_P_Value to Raw_P
lead_snp[, c("SNP_ID", "Position", "Raw_P")]
#Here, "lead SNP" refers to the strongest signal in our analysis.


# Define the region: 500 kb on each side
window_bp <- 500000

region_start <- max(1, lead_snp$Position - window_bp)
region_end <- lead_snp$Position + window_bp

# Select tested SNPs inside this region
# (Removed the Chromosome check since all data is on Chromosome 10 anyway)
region_results <- valid_results[
    valid_results$Position >= region_start &
    valid_results$Position <= region_end,
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]

# Sort SNPs by genomic position
region_results <- region_results[
  order(region_results$Position),
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]

nrow(region_results)

# How many SNPs in the region have a reliable test and how many are flagged
table(region_results$Status)
  
# Select controls and SNPs from the chosen region
is_control <- phenotype == 0

region_genotypes <- genotypes_clean[
  is_control,
  region_results$SNP_ID,
  drop = FALSE
]

# Extract the lead SNP genotypes
lead_genotype <- region_genotypes[[lead_snp$SNP_ID]]

dim(region_genotypes)

# Prepare result columns
region_results$LD_r2 <- NA_real_
region_results$LD_n <- 0L
region_results$LD_status <- "Not calculated"

#Calculate LD for each SNP
for (i in seq_len(ncol(region_genotypes))) {

  other_genotype <- region_genotypes[[i]]

  complete_pair <- !is.na(lead_genotype) &
                   !is.na(other_genotype)

  region_results$LD_n[i] <- sum(complete_pair)

  if (sum(complete_pair) < 3) {
    region_results$LD_status[i] <- "Too few observations"
    next
  }

  x <- lead_genotype[complete_pair]
  y <- other_genotype[complete_pair]

  if (var(x) == 0 || var(y) == 0) {
    region_results$LD_status[i] <- "Zero variance"
    next
  }

  region_results$LD_r2[i] <- cor(x, y)^2
  region_results$LD_status[i] <- "Calculated"
}

#check results
table(region_results$LD_status)

range(region_results$LD_n)

region_results[
  order(region_results$LD_r2, decreasing = TRUE),
  c("SNP_ID", "Position", "LD_r2", "LD_n")
][1:6, ]


#A plot combining SNP position, strength of association, and LD with the lead SNP
# Assign colours according to LD with the lead SNP
point_colours <- rep("grey85", nrow(region_results))

known_ld <- !is.na(region_results$LD_r2)

point_colours[known_ld] <- "grey50"

point_colours[
  known_ld & region_results$LD_r2 >= 0.2
] <- "orange"

point_colours[
  known_ld & region_results$LD_r2 >= 0.8
] <- "red"

# Convert p-values to plot heights (Changed Raw_P_Value to Raw_P)
association_height <- -log10(region_results$Raw_P)

# Include the Bonferroni threshold in the plotting range
bonf_height <- -log10(decision_threshold)
y_upper <- max(c(association_height, bonf_height)) + 0.8

# Plot association evidence and LD
plot(
  region_results$Position / 1e6,
  association_height,
  pch = 19,
  col = point_colours,
  ylim = c(0, y_upper),
  xlab = "Position on chromosome 10 (Mb)",
  ylab = expression(-log[10](p)),
  main = paste("Region around", lead_snp$SNP_ID)
)

# Show the primary multiple-testing threshold
abline(h = bonf_height, col = "red", lty = 2)

# Highlight the lead SNP (Changed Raw_P_Value to Raw_P)
points(
  lead_snp$Position / 1e6,
  -log10(lead_snp$Raw_P),
  pch = 18,
  col = "purple",
  cex = 1.5
)

legend(
  "topright",
  legend = c(
    "LD r² < 0.2",
    "0.2 ≤ LD r² < 0.8",
    "LD r² ≥ 0.8",
    "LD unavailable",
    "Lead SNP",
    "Bonferroni threshold"
  ),
  col = c("grey50", "orange", "red", "grey85", "purple", "red"),
  pch = c(19, 19, 19, 19, 18, NA),
  lty = c(NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, 2),
  cex = 0.7,
  bg = "white"
)

```

# Comments

This code evaluates the lead SNP—the one with the lowest p-value—designating it as the reference. Then, a 1 Mb window centered on the lead SNP is defined, and the LD is computed by calculating the squared correlation (r^2) between the lead SNP and every other SNP in the selected cohort. This value explains how strongly the variants are correlated.Finally, an informative regional plot is displayed. It shows the physical position on the chromosome on the x-axis, while the association strength on the y-axis uses the -log_10(p) scale. Four categories of colors are used for the LD: red for strong correlation, orange for moderate correlation, dark grey for low correlation, and light grey when LD is unavailable. The lead SNP is marked with a purple diamond. The Bonferroni threshold distinguishes significant elements from non-significant ones.

We can conclude that nearby associated SNPs do not represent independent effects. In fact, as shown in the plot, the medium/high-ranking dots near the peak are located close to each other in the genome and show local correlation. This shows they aren't independent, they are simply inherited together in the same block of DNA.
While the lead SNP designates the strongest statistical association in the region, it is rarely guaranteed to be the true causal variant. Because correlation spans across the local LD block, a group of neighboring variants will share similar significance levels, meaning the true causal mutation could be any one of them.

### Interpretation of the regional LD analysis

The plot shows association evidence and LD around the lead SNP, rs2776932. Genomic position is shown on the x-axis, while −log10(p) indicates association strength on the y-axis. Colours represent squared genotype correlations with the lead SNP, estimated in controls. The purple diamond marks the lead SNP, and the dashed red line shows the Bonferroni threshold.

The nearby SNP rs2776934 has very high LD with rs2776932 (r² ≈ 0.987). Several other neighbouring variants show intermediate LD. Therefore, nearby association signals should not automatically be interpreted as independent effects: correlated variants may carry overlapping information. However, this analysis does not establish that all variants belong to one haplotype block or that there is only one underlying effect.

No variant in the region passes the Bonferroni threshold. Additionally, 49 regional variants have association tests flagged for expected counts below five, so their asymptotic p-values require caution.

The SNP with the smallest p-value is not necessarily causal. It may be correlated with another variant through LD, or the observed signal may reflect sampling variation. A causal variant, if present, could also be absent from the dataset.

LD pruning for PCA reduces the disproportionate influence of correlated SNPs on the principal components. Association testing has a different purpose: it evaluates individual variants. SNPs removed from the PCA subset can therefore remain in the association analysis, where their correlations help interpret neighbouring signals.



# 5. Assess robustness

Choose one scientifically motivated sensitivity analysis, such as changing a QC threshold or evaluating a different genetic model. Explain your choice before inspecting its results. Keep the primary analysis identifiable and account for any change in the number of tested variants.


**Decision to explain:** Which conclusions remain stable, which change, and what explains the change?

# Explanation of our robustness assessment

For our sensitivity analysis, we decided to investigate whether our strict 10% Minor Allele Frequency (MAF) threshold prematurely discarded variants that were actually associated with the disease. 
To assess this, we bypassed the MAF filter, effectively evaluating all variants that passed the initial missingness QC.
Testing rare variants is tricky because low allele counts create sparse contingency tables, which can invalidate standard Chi-squared tests and yield unreliable p-values. To handle this, we used a two-step approach: we first screened all rare variants with a standard test while tracking minimum expected cell counts, and then re-tested any nominally significant variants (p < 0.05) using Monte Carlo simulations (with 2,000 permutations) to get reliable empirical p-values. Lastly, we adjusted our Bonferroni threshold to account for the total number of tested variants (m_total), making sure we evaluated any potential rare variant signals under appropriately strict significance criteria.

```{r message = FALSE, results='hold', warning=FALSE}
# ==========================================
# 5. SENSITIVITY ANALYSIS: RARE VARIANTS & MONTE CARLO SIMULATION
# ==========================================

# 1. Isolate the variants that passed missingness but were discarded by the MAF < 10% filter
rare_snps_idx <- pass_snp_miss & !pass_maf
genotypes_rare <- study_data[, c(FALSE, FALSE, rare_snps_idx)]

cat("Testing", ncol(genotypes_rare), "rare variants excluded in the primary analysis.\n")

# 2. Fast asymptotic screening on rare variants
# The function returns the p-value and the smallest expected count,
# so that we can say how many tests are unreliable (sparse tables)
# What is the meaning of the retrieved p-values?
# Normally, tiny p-value suggests that the distribution of that variant (0, 1, 2) is
# drastically different between cases and controls while a high p-value suggests
# no evidence of an association.
# By choosing to not apply a MAF threshold and considering rare variants, as done in this part,
# a small p-values suggest a sort of artifact because low allele counts create 
#   sparse contingency tables that invalidate standard asymptotic tests.
test_rare_asympt <- function(snp_vector) {
  valid_idx <- !is.na(snp_vector) & !is.na(phenotype)
  s <- snp_vector[valid_idx]
  p <- phenotype[valid_idx]
  if (length(unique(s)) <= 1 || length(unique(p)) <= 1) {
    return(c(p_value = NA, min_expected = NA))
  }
  tbl <- table(s, p)
  fit <- suppressWarnings(chisq.test(tbl, correct = FALSE))
  c(p_value = fit$p.value, min_expected = min(fit$expected))
}

rare_out <- t(sapply(genotypes_rare, test_rare_asympt))
rare_p_vals <- rare_out[, "p_value"]
rare_min_exp <- rare_out[, "min_expected"]

# How reliable is the screening?
cat("Rare variants tested:", sum(!is.na(rare_p_vals)), "\n")
cat("Rare variants not testable (no variation):", sum(is.na(rare_p_vals)), "\n")
cat("Tests with a minimum expected count < 5 (asymptotic p-value not reliable):",
    sum(rare_min_exp < 5, na.rm = TRUE), "\n")

# 3. Update the Multiple Testing penalty for the full set
# In the following part, a new Bonferroni threshold is computed. 
# This new threshold takes into account the larger number of variants 
# compared to the previous Bonferroni threshold.
m_total <- sum(pass_snp_miss)  # primary variants + rare variants
new_bonf_threshold <- 0.05 / m_total

cat("\n=== Sensitivity Analysis Results ===\n")
cat("Original Bonferroni threshold (m =", sum(pass_snp), "):", 0.05 / sum(pass_snp), "\n")
cat("New strict Bonferroni threshold (m =", m_total, "):", new_bonf_threshold, "\n")

# Check if any rare variant passes the Bonferroni threshold.
# At this point, we evaluate if any of the newly considered variants have a p-value
# smaller than the new Bonferroni threshold. If this happens, it means that some 
# highly significant rare variant was accidentally discarded by the primary MAF filter.
sig_rare_count <- sum(rare_p_vals <= new_bonf_threshold, na.rm = TRUE)
cat("Rare variants passing new Bonferroni threshold:", sig_rare_count, "\n")
cat("Smallest asymptotic p-value among rare variants:",
    signif(min(rare_p_vals, na.rm = TRUE), 3), "\n")

# The primary result is compared with the new threshold too
cat("Primary analysis: smallest raw p-value", signif(min(results_table$Raw_P, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    "vs new threshold", signif(new_bonf_threshold, 3), "\n")
# No rare variant passes the new bonferroni threshold

# 4. Monte Carlo simulation only for nominally significant rare variants (p < 0.05)
# It is a reliability check of the smallest p-values, not a test that can confirm
# Bonferroni significance (with B = 2000 the smallest possible p-value is 1/2001,
# about 5e-4, larger than the threshold)
nominally_sig_rare <- which(rare_p_vals < 0.05)
cat("Rare variants requiring Monte Carlo verification (p < 0.05):", length(nominally_sig_rare), "\n")

if (length(nominally_sig_rare) > 0) {
  set.seed(20261031)
  mc_p_vals <- numeric(length(nominally_sig_rare))
  for (j in seq_along(nominally_sig_rare)) {
    snp_col <- genotypes_rare[[nominally_sig_rare[j]]]
    valid_idx <- !is.na(snp_col) & !is.na(phenotype)
    tbl <- table(snp_col[valid_idx], phenotype[valid_idx])
    mc_p_vals[j] <- chisq.test(tbl, simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 2000)$p.value
  }
  cat("Smallest Monte Carlo p-value among rare variants:", signif(min(mc_p_vals), 3), "\n")
}
# The smallest resulting empirical p-value was 5e-04 (the lower bound for 2,000 permutations). 
# Since this value remains well above the strict Bonferroni threshold, we confirm that 
# these rare variants do not reach true significance, validating our 10% MAF filter.


```

# Conclusion about our Sensitivity Analysis
Our sensitivity analysis proves that our 10% MAF filter was the right call. When we went back and tested all the rare variants we initially dropped, none of them came close to passing our strict Bonferroni significance cutoff. The few rare variants that initially looked slightly interesting (p < 0.05) turned out to be false alarms caused by low sample counts in sparse tables, which our Monte Carlo simulations quickly cleared up.
